ambient-section-particles: Use when a region should feel like it holds a medium: slow drifting motes with tunable density, downward pull, sideways drift, sway and spin, either recycling forever, leaving, settling into a shallow pile, or frozen as a still arrangement, hinting at temperature, flow or scale behind content that stays primary. It saves you from motes that teleport after the tab was hidden, duplicated loops after a remount, density picked from window width instead of the region's area, and drift that quietly eats text contrast. Generic motes only; recognizable tumbling objects and pointer-drawn trails are separate.
animation-systems: Use when the question is how motion should behave across an entire page rather than how to make one thing move: what leads and what follows, how long each class of change should last, which curves to reuse everywhere, and which movements to cut because they carry no meaning. It supplies the numbers, durations scaled to the size of the change, the gap between staggered items, exits quicker than entrances, and the rule that a reduced-motion preference must leave content visible rather than hidden. It sets the policy; the moving itself is carried out by other skills.
animejs: Use when one motion must be distributed across many elements at once, arriving one after another or rippling outward from the center of a grid, or when a drawn line must trace itself out as though being written and one outline must flow into another shape, with the whole run pausable, reversible, and seekable to any moment. Compared with a plain sequencing timeline, that spread and that self-drawing are the point. It saves you from offsets misread as absolute moments, values that silently do nothing for want of a unit, and loops that outlive their page.
atmosphere-background: Use when a dark field needs weather and direction: soft folds of light drifting slowly across the frame like illuminated fabric, overlapping so crossings brighten, with the glow pooling toward one corner or lower edge so the frame has a focal area instead of even brightness. Backdrop only — it stops where the background must carry structure, discrete drifting motes, or one dominating beam. It saves you from a flat multi-stop wash with no layered fold structure, from a uniform full-frame glow that competes with foreground, and from a fixed cyan cast when the page has its own accent.
babylonjs-engine: Use when a three-dimensional scene must also behave: things falling under gravity, colliding, resting, hinged, shoved, picked, with imported rigged figures playing their own motion and controls drawn inside the scene. It reaches a small self-contained world with orbiting or walk-through viewpoints, cast shadows, and quality that steps down when frames slip; one solid turning quietly needs far less. It saves you from bodies that ignore gravity because simulation was never switched on, viewpoints that never answer input, models asked for before they arrive, repeated objects each charged full price, and scenes that leak because removing is not releasing.
background-grid-webgl: Use when the backdrop should feel like space receding away — a ruled ground plane drifting toward a distant horizon, its lines thinning and dissolving with distance, a sparse dust of floating motes, and a gentle sway that answers the pointer — so foreground content sits inside depth rather than on a flat panel. It owns only the backdrop layer and stays restrained rather than bright retro neon. Saves you from the failures that ruin it: linework heavy enough to fight the text, haze thick enough to hide the structure, and pointer response so eager the background feels unstable.
barba-js: Use when a reader moves between separate whole pages and the handover should feel continuous — the outgoing page animating away, the incoming one arriving, no blank flash and no persistent frame around them jumping. It coordinates the exchange and lets each pair of pages have its own handover, but it governs only the crossing between documents, not motion inside one. It saves you from the swap firing before the exit finishes, the arriving page flashing at full strength, the two pages stacking and shoving layout when they overlap, and whatever the departing page started running forever.
cobejs: Use when a small, continuously turning Earth should sit in a corner or a card as a compact visual anchor, marked with a handful of locations as glowing dots and either drifting on its own or turning under the pointer. It stops short of connections, territories, routes, or values painted across land, anything where the map itself carries the argument. It saves you from a globe that renders soft and blurry because its drawing resolution never matched its displayed size, that stays the wrong size after its container changes, or that keeps spinning after removal.
container-lines: Use when the page's own measurements should be visible — hairline vertical guides standing at the edges of the content column, with tiny exact marks at true corners — so a composition reads as deliberately measured rather than loosely placed. It gives quiet structural tension to a layout that feels adrift and stays framing; it never illustrates or explains a structure. It saves you from guides that miss the real column edge because they were sized separately from it, widths that change from section to section, marks landing on arbitrary points, and framing that swallows clicks, hovers, and text selection.
corner-diagonals: Use when panels, cards, and controls should read as machined or cut rather than softly rounded, with angled corners repeated as one consistent structural language across a page. It governs how large a cut should be relative to each component and how framed surfaces stay legible once clipped. It saves you from the mistakes that make it look broken instead of deliberate: an angled fill still sitting inside a rectangular outline and rectangular clickable area, text crowded into the slope, sibling components cut by different amounts, and focus indication lost around the clipped silhouette.
corner-lasers: Use when light should enter the field from one off-center anchor at a corner or edge: two or three thin beams sharing a single origin, a white-hot junction that is the brightest point on the page, and haze that seems lit by that point rather than blanketing everything. It saves you from unrelated lines that merely happen to cross, cores thickened into neon bars because the core and its halo were tuned together, fog with no relationship to the source, and a default cold blue that ignores the accent color. Centered dominant beams belong elsewhere.
css-alpha-masking: Use when an element's edge should dissolve into transparency instead of ending on a hard line: a list running past its container, a diagram continuing beyond its frame, a travelling band of terms fading out at both ends, an image melting into the background. You choose the direction the fade runs and how deep it eats inward, and partial rather than full transparency gives a gentler edge. It changes visibility only, never sharpness, so a gradual softening of focus is a different job. It saves you from a fade that silently does nothing in one major browser family.
css-border-gradient: Use when an edge must change colour along its length, so a rim catches light on one side or a directional highlight marks the one panel that matters, which a flat outline cannot express. It gives a surface a premium boundary at hairline weight, quieter than the content it frames, one hierarchy level at a time. It treats the edge only: not a glowing frame, not a travelling band, not depth. Saves you from an edge that wipes out the panel's own backdrop, corner curvature that misregisters, transparency tuned on dark that reads wrong on light, and doubled outlines.
d3-viz: Use when a picture must be computed from data rather than drawn by hand: nodes joined by links, hierarchies, flows, circular relationship rings, grids colored by value, or shapes placed onto a map projection, with every position, size, color and transition under exact control. It carries the arithmetic that turns values into drawing coordinates, keeps axis labels from being clipped by the frame, redraws cleanly instead of stacking duplicates each time the data changes, and settles network layouts by simulated attraction. Everything stays flat; volume and camera depth belong elsewhere.
design-taste-frontend: Use when a page needs a committed visual direction chosen before layout: reading audience and mood, then fixing type scale, spacing rhythm, one locked accent, and varied section composition so nothing reads as generated default. Also for reworking an existing look. It saves you from tells: a small uppercase label above every heading, repeated alternating text-and-picture rows, invented precise-sounding figures, headlines outgrowing the first screen, accent and corner-rounding drift between sections. Siblings apply one ready-made palette or one named surface look; this decides the whole direction, then audits mechanically. It stops at dense instrument panels and data grids.
dither-background: Use when a backdrop should look sampled and quantized: visibly enlarged square cells, a repeating threshold pattern, broad slow-drifting cloud masses in near-black and gray, with edges falling off so one bright mass sits off-center. It saves you from the two failures that ruin it, cells so small the ordered pattern collapses into grain, and brightness redrawn randomly each frame so the field flickers instead of drifting. Cheapness comes from enlarging the cells, not thinning the field. Monochrome atmosphere behind content only, with no color, no depth cues and nothing to interact with.
falling-leaves: Use when many small flat objects must tumble on their own axes as they fall — showing a face, thinning to nothing edge-on, opening out again — so the drift reads as real things moving through air rather than shapes sliding downward. It carries recognisable identity and layered depth, a few crossing in front of the words; shapeless motes are a question of atmosphere instead. It saves you from the one detail whose absence makes it confetti, from sideways travel untied from the tumble that reads as a bug, from matching front and back faces, from a shared rhythm the eye catches in seconds, and from counts that blizzard on a small screen.
frontend-design: Use when one page's look must be decided rather than defaulted: which palette, which display and body type pairing, what layout, the single element it will be remembered by, and the wording, which betrays a templated page as fast as the visuals. It draws those choices from the subject's own world and makes you criticise the plan before building. It shapes one page's character; it neither hands down a shared identity for a whole set nor reworks an existing site. Saves you from the few looks machine-made design keeps reproducing, and from spacing rules that cancel each other.
glass-dark-ui: Use when panels must float translucently over a dark or moving backdrop while the words on them stay fully readable — frosted surfaces, a rim catching light along one edge, restrained depth and glow. It sets the whole dark surface vocabulary, backdrop through muted text, with the contrast floors that keep it legible; it treats the panels, never the scene behind them. It saves you from body text that dissolves once the background moves, glow so wide it eats its own label, dead-black overlays that go muddy, focus states lost in the haze, and panels unreadable wherever translucency is not honoured.
globe-gl: Use when the subject is spread across the real Earth and where a thing sits on the sphere carries the meaning — cities as marked points, links as arcs arching between them, territories shaded by value, routes over land, labels pinned to coordinates. It stacks several such layers on one turnable sphere; an abstract ball of lights standing for a network, or a small ornamental spinner with a few pins, are different asks. It saves you from a sphere that collapses because its holder was never sized, overlays lost against a bright surface, and counts that stall small devices.
globe-particles: Use when a sphere assembled from thousands of glowing points, slowly turning and tilted inside an orbital ring or flattened disc, should stand in abstractly for a system, a network, or a field. It carries no real places, coordinates, or labels, so any subject where position on the sphere itself carries meaning belongs elsewhere. It saves you from the two failures that ruin the effect: glow pushed so far that the silhouette dissolves into a bright blur, and points scattered so evenly that the shape reads as a loose star field rather than a sphere with an orbit.
gooey-blob-system: Use when separate soft shapes must actually merge into one mass and pull apart again — cells dividing, droplets joining, a neck that stretches thin and finally snaps — rather than you drawing each merged outline by hand. The union happens automatically as the shapes approach, so motion stays continuous and fluid. It handles rounded organic forms, not rigid bodies, collisions, or measured quantities. Saves you from the imposter version, blurred circles that overlap without ever fusing, and from spacing, softness and contrast drifting apart until the merging stops being visible.
gsap-core: Use when a single value must change over time with exact control over its curve, delay, repetition, direction, and what happens when it finishes — more than a plain state-to-state transition can express. It covers one movement, or the same movement staggered across a set of items; ordering several movements against each other belongs to the timeline sibling. It saves you from animating the properties that force the page to re-lay-out, from leaving faded-out things still catching clicks, from a second entrance animation silently cancelling the first, and from ignoring a reader who has asked for less motion.
gsap-scrolltrigger: Use when a sequence's progress must be steered by a continuously changing value the reader controls — a position, a slider, a page's travel — so motion advances, holds and rewinds exactly as that value moves, and a scene can stay held in place while the value runs on, snapping to named moments. It saves you from two animations fighting over the same property and jumping, from a whole group firing at once instead of each element on its own arrival, and from stale positions after the frame is resized. Stops short of motion that simply plays on its own clock.
gsap-timeline: Use when several movements must be arranged against each other in time — this one starting slightly before that one ends, three overlapping, a named moment you can jump to — and the whole arrangement then played, paused, reversed, restarted, or scrubbed to any point as one unit. It handles ordering and grouping, including sequences nested inside sequences; a single movement, or progress driven by a continuous input like scroll, belongs to its siblings. It saves you from hand-computed waiting periods that all break the moment one step's length changes.
lightweight-3d-effects: Use when a page needs a hint of depth without real three-dimensional geometry: a card that tips toward the pointer with layered inner planes and a moving sheen, or a rounded illustration assembled from primitives that spins and can be dragged. Ready-made animated backdrops come along, though a sibling covers those alone more deeply. It carries tasteful tilt ranges, the teardown that stops abandoned instances leaking, why such an illustration renders blank, and why a second animated backdrop halves the frame rate. Stops where orbitable geometry, lighting and imported models begin.
locomotive-scroll: Use when a tall page should glide with weight and inertia instead of jumping line by line, and layers should travel at different speeds so depth is felt while reading. It also reports how far each region has entered view, pins elements within a region, and can turn vertical input into sideways travel. It takes over the page's own scrolling wholesale — heavier than merely revealing items as they arrive. Saves you from pinned things drifting off, stale positions after content changes, and readers who dislike altered scrolling being stuck with it.
lottie-animations: Use when a finished, hand-crafted vector animation should play on the page without anyone re-creating its motion frame by frame, and such an asset exists or can be obtained: a character that moves, an icon transforming, a looping illustration. It stays crisp at any size, loops, and can be paused, scrubbed to an exact moment, limited to one segment, recoloured or slowed. It stops where the motion must be invented or driven by data. Saves you from assets whose glows and depth silently vanish on arrival, ones heavy enough to stutter, and copies that keep running unseen.
make-illustration: Use when a page needs a picture of something that has no photograph and no exact geometry — an atmosphere, a setting, a material, a metaphor, a stylised object standing in for an idea — and drawing it by hand would cost more than it returns. It produces a finished picture beside the page in one step, and can hold a whole set to one look. It stops hard at two places: anything whose correctness the reader will check, and anything that must carry readable words or numbers, since those come out wrong often enough to be untrustworthy. For anything that really exists and was photographed, the sibling that retrieves real material is the honest choice.
marquee-loop: Use when a strip of items, terms, examples, small pictures, tags, should travel across the page endlessly with no visible seam, restart or jump, as one continuous ambient band. It carries repeating or glanceable material at a steady pace, and can ease off while the reader points at it. It stops being right for anything that must be read carefully, since each item passes and cannot be recalled. Saves you from a band that visibly snaps to the start, items that jitter when widths vary, hard edges where they pop in, and motion forced on readers who asked for less.
matterjs: Use when things must fall, collide, swing, stack, topple, settle, or be dragged with convincing weight and momentum in a flat side-on world — a pendulum, a lever, a rope, colliding carts, a pile that collapses — so motion emerges from mass and force rather than being scripted. Outcomes cannot be dictated frame by frame; a movement that must land exactly where you say belongs to the sequencing siblings. It saves you from hand-written motion that drifts and jitters, objects passing straight through each other, and everything falling out of view forever because nothing bounds the world.
mini-game: Use when a concept only lands by doing: a playable unit with one goal, one core action, feedback, a win or lose condition and a reset, delivered as a self-contained embeddable piece that reports its state and result. It saves you from inventing scores the model does not define, from state scattered across the drawing instead of one object every action passes through, from baking instructions, buttons or numbers into the artwork, and from defaulting to generic placeholder shapes when the subject calls for a tangible world, exact geometry, or a purely numeric board.
pixijs-2d: Use when a page must animate thousands of tiny elements at once — drifting point fields, sparks, swarms, streaks — and animating that many ordinary page elements would visibly stutter. You author the behaviour yourself: spawning, recycling and steering each item, drawing shapes procedurally, and layering image-wide visual treatments. Choose a ready-made ambient effect instead when one fixed look suffices, and something else for depth-lit three-dimensional scenes or true collision response. Saves you from the memory growth and per-item update costs that make large counts crawl after a minute.
pointer-trail-emitter: Use when something must be laid down along the path a pointer travels — a trail, a brush stroke — with the same spacing whether the hand flicks or crawls. It covers even deposition, drift and fade after landing, and a faint breath under a resting hand. It saves you from spacing tied to the clock, which scatters a flick into dots and piles a still hand into a column; from a frame's worth dumped at one end of a flick; and from thousands appearing at once when the pointer jumps. It marks; it does not stir an existing field.
progressive-blur: Use when blur must grow gradually across a strip so whatever passes beneath dissolves smoothly toward an edge, instead of a hard line where sharp content suddenly becomes soft. Typical uses: letting a heading sit legibly over busy imagery, or fading the top or bottom of a scene under an overlay. You control the direction, height, and how strong the softening gets. It softens what already exists behind it, so a flat empty area shows nothing. Saves you from the visible banding of a single abrupt step and from the strip swallowing clicks meant for the content beneath.
reveal-hover-effect: Use when two aligned versions of the same picture must be compared by uncovering one through the other under a moving pointer: before and after, outside and inside, raw and processed. It handles the hard parts, keeping both versions pixel-identical so the boundary never betrays a mismatch, starting the opening under the cursor instead of sweeping in from the middle, keeping it attached while the page scrolls, and collapsing it when attention leaves. One soft-edged region at a time, requiring a pointer; anything essential needs a non-hover route. Unlike a fixed edge fade, the opening follows the hand.
scroll-reveal-libraries: Use when the only motion needed is content becoming visible as it comes into view — fading, sliding, zooming or flipping in, declared per element, with staggered arrival delays if you want a rough cascade. It saves you from re-measuring by hand after new content appears (freshly added items stay invisible until you ask for a recount), from durations past a few seconds being silently ignored, and from guessing which part of an element crossing which part of the frame fires it. Each element runs alone; there is no shared clock to pause, reverse or seek.
skeuomorphic-ui: Use when a control should read as a physical object you could press or turn — a moulded surface catching light along its top edge, darkening below, sitting proudly above the page or carved into it, with a faint reflective rim and texture you feel more than see. Covers cards, buttons, switches, dials, and toolbars, including the pressed state where depth reverses. Saves you from the tells of a fake: light arriving from several directions at once, sooty black shadows, blending it with translucent glass surfaces in the same component, and texture so coarse that small controls turn muddy.
technical-wireframe-info-layout: Use when a whole page should read as an annotated technical plate: the subject pulled apart into separated components with thin routed lines running out to sparse labels and metric readouts, on a near-black restrained palette where emphasis comes from brightness, line weight and spacing rather than colour, with slow analytical drift. It governs layout, typography, labels and the centrepiece together, not one decorative layer. It saves you from an outlined object that becomes unrelated background art, from labels multiplying until the structure is unreadable, and from a solid glossy rendering that hides the parts you were separating.
theme-factory: Use when a set of separate pages must look like one designed system rather than a run of unrelated experiments: a single coordinated palette, one heading-and-body type pairing, one surface treatment, applied identically to every one of them, or when such an identity must be invented and then held to. Ten fully worked identities are ready to pick from, each already balanced for contrast and readability, and a new one can be built and reviewed first. It settles the shared vocabulary only; how each page is composed stays open. Saves you from pages that drift apart one by one.
threejs-landscape: Use when a subject needs to be standing somewhere: open ground stretching to a horizon, sky above it, grass and stones near the viewer, a time of day that can slide from dawn to night. It is scenery that reads at a glance and then recedes — weather layered on top and buildings standing in it are separate siblings. It saves you from detail spread evenly instead of concentrated where the eye is, ground tinted by a repeating picture that announces itself, far hills flattening out, scattered things floating above or sinking below the surface, and time-of-day changes that jump.
threejs-towers: Use when a structure should build itself on screen in named stages rather than appear finished — tiers stacking, a temporary support frame always one step ahead of the finished work — so growth or accumulation reads as a sequence. Best when the form is made of repeated, parameterised parts. It saves you from vanishing surfaces built facing the wrong way, from a rising cut line that leaves the body hollow unless the exposed cross-section is capped to the shape it is crossing, from steps that read as floating shelves, and from interior light leaking along the silhouette.
threejs-weather: Use when precipitation must read as real weather across a dimensional scene: rain whose single drops you can follow, a storm that leans with the wind, lightning whose thunder arrives late and softer with distance, a blizzard that swells and passes, snow that visibly deepens on the ground while it keeps falling. It layers weather onto a scene built elsewhere, and does not make the terrain or structures beneath it. Saves you from drops falling where the view never looks, storms rebuilt as a second unrelated system, flashes that wash the text out, and arriving mid-whiteout every time.
threejs-webgl: Use when the subject genuinely needs three dimensions the reader can orbit around: a structure with real depth, lit surfaces, cast shadows, materials that answer to light, and parts that respond when pointed at. It carries a whole scene: camera framing, lighting arrangement, imported models, thousands of repeated bodies, staged viewpoint moves. It stops short of bodies that fall and collide on their own, and is heavy where a flat suggestion of depth would do. Saves you from washed-out colour, flickering coincident surfaces, shadows switched on in only one of three needed places, and scenes that hoard memory.
vantajs: Use when a section needs a living ambient backdrop chosen from a small catalogue of ready-made looks — rolling waves, drifting fog, a connected net of points, clouds, cells — tuned by colour, scale and speed rather than authored motion by motion. It loops forever and carries no meaning about the content in front of it; a backdrop that must express a specific idea has to be built. It saves you from a host region with no measured size showing nothing, from several such backdrops at once bogging the machine down, and from text sinking into the churn behind it.
web-access: 所有联网操作必须通过此 skill 处理，包括：搜索、网页抓取、登录后操作、网络交互等。 触发场景：用户要求搜索信息、查看网页内容、访问需要登录的网站、操作网页界面、抓取社交媒体内容（小红书、微博、推特等）、读取动态渲染页面、以及任何需要真实浏览器环境的网络任务。
web-media-getter: Use when a page needs the real thing rather than an impression of it — a named person, a documented place, an event that happened, a museum object, a specimen, an instrument — where an invented picture would misrepresent the evidence. It gathers candidates from free archival and public collections, brings them down beside the page, and records for each one where it came from and on what terms, which is the part that cannot be reconstructed afterwards. It stops at anything abstract that no camera ever pointed at; inventing those is the sibling's job.
webgl-3d-object: Use when one object should read as a genuine solid — a form whose lit faces, highlights, edges and cast shadow shift as it slowly turns — rather than a flat drawing of a three-dimensional shape. It is a single showpiece object floating in an otherwise empty frame, not a scene, a place, or something the reader steers. It saves you from a shadow side that goes dead black, a silhouette that disappears against the background without a light from behind, a projection that flattens the depth away, and a form that stretches when the frame changes shape.
webgl-laser: Use when one intense beam of light should own the whole field — a needle-thin white-hot core, a narrow coloured halo, and slow-drifting haze that blooms beside it and thins outward — as a full-screen backdrop behind everything else. It gives you one beam, not a light show; multiple accent streaks at the corners or a general glow field are different jobs. Saves you from the versions that read wrong: a beam thick enough to look like a bar, fog that spreads evenly instead of hugging the beam, flicker, and colour that ignores the page's accent.
